title: A hypergeometric event law gives exact interval-shuffle tests for long-to-short bursts
abstract: Under uniform permutations of a fixed interval histogram, long-to-short burst event counts have a hypergeometric law. Given the event count, extra burst spikes have a beta-binomial law. We derive the joint law, exact tail tests, a conditional chain test, a direct sampler and independent-stratum convolution. All 265,720 interval-label words through length 11 matched the joint formula in exact integer arithmetic. In 15 fixed synthetic histograms, a nominal 5 percent normal upper-tail test rejected up to 18.1 percent of null orders; exact tests stayed at or below 5 percent. A 20-shuffle naive tail reached 9.13 percent, while the plus-one tail stayed below 5 percent. Exact pooled tests still failed in a two-state counterexample, while stratum tests retained control. This extends prior exact moments to count distributions. It adds no animal data and does not establish wiring or channel effects. Exchangeability, fixed thresholds and valid state partitions remain necessary. Floating-point extreme tails and large supports need care. Code, proof, tables and figures reproduce without external data.

display.caption: Exact null rejection rates for 15 fixed histograms. Normal and naive small-shuffle tails can be liberal.
Pooling two fixed rate states gives a false burst deficit. Independent state-specific permutations retain calibration.

citations.reason: We extend its gap representation and exact moments to a full joint count law and finite-sample tails.
Its long-to-short-chain burst rule and 20-shuffle means motivate the count test. No biological data are reused.
Prior tests for burst and pause detection.
